Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Non-profit Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Vignette:
Rajesh still remembers the night it happened - the sound of his bedroom door creaking open, the feeling of being pinned down, and the voice whispering cruel things in his ear. It was a voice he knew all too well, one that had been supposed to be a source of comfort and support. The memories of that night are still fragmented, but certain sounds - the rustling of sheets, the creaking of floorboards - can transport him back to that moment with alarming clarity. When these memories surface, Rajesh often feels a searing pain in his lower back, where he was injured during the assault. In the aftermath, Rajesh found himself withdrawing from the world around him. As a non-profit worker, he had always thrived on human connection and community, but now being alone in a room or building filled him with an unshakeable sense of unease. He began to avoid meetings at his office, opting instead for remote work arrangements that allowed him to stay isolated. When he did venture out, he would position himself strategically, sitting with his back against the wall so that he could see the entire room - a habit born of the need to constantly monitor potential threats. The slightest touch from someone else could send Rajesh's heart racing. He flinched at the gentle brush of an arm or hand, his body primed for fight-or-flight. At home, he would find himself standing stock-still in the hallway, straining to listen for any sounds that might signal someone's approach - a creaking floorboard, the rustling of fabric. Loud noises made him jump: car horns, slamming doors, or even the shrill ringtone of his phone. Rajesh had trouble articulating what happened that night. When memories surfaced, he often felt like he was drowning in a sea of emotions - anger, shame, and despair swirling together into an overwhelming tide. He knew intellectually that it wasn't his fault, but a nagging voice inside whispered that he must have somehow invited this horror upon himself. "I am permanently an outsider now," he thought to himself, unable to shake the feeling of being somehow tainted by what had occurred. Physical pain became an all-too-familiar companion for Rajesh. When memories of the assault returned, his body would tense up, and the ache in his lower back would intensify. It was as if his body was screaming at him to pay attention, to stay vigilant against threats that lurked around every corner. To cope with these feelings of overwhelm, Rajesh began engaging in self-harming behaviors - cutting himself or slamming his fists into walls in a desperate bid for release. As time went on, the world around Rajesh began to shrink. He stopped attending social gatherings and eventually severed ties with friends who couldn't understand why he'd become so withdrawn. His work performance suffered as well; colleagues grew concerned about his increasing isolationism, but Rajesh just felt like he was barely holding it together. It's been two years since the assault, and Rajesh is finally seeking help - pushed by a deepening sense of despair that things will never get better. He hopes therapy can teach him to quiet the cacophony in his head, to learn to tolerate the presence of others without freaking out. Mostly, he yearns for some semblance of peace - an end to the constant threat monitoring and hypervigilance that's consumed his life since that fateful night.
